posts.post_text: We banned ChatGPT in our analytics department last month. Not because AI is bad — because nobody could explain where the numbers came from. When a regulator asks 'how did you arrive at this figure?' and the answer is 'GPT said so', you've got a compliance problem. The AI trust gap is real and growing.
posts.angle: High-scoring post with three ICP prospects engaging — validate the compliance-driven trust gap, and add the insight that the problem isn't AI output but AI explainability, without pitching
posts.draft_comment: The ban makes complete sense to me. It's not really an AI problem — it's an audit trail problem. Most tools will give you a number, very few will tell you the story behind it in a way that holds up when someone senior starts asking questions. I wonder how many analytics teams are quietly in the same position but haven't had the regulator moment yet.

posts.post_text: We spent 18 months building a Power BI dashboard that our finance team refuses to use. They still export everything to Excel and email it around. The building part was easy. Getting people to actually trust the numbers enough to quote them in a board meeting? That's the real challenge nobody talks about. Anyone else hit this wall?
posts.angle: ICP prospect COO at 140-person firm hitting the classic adoption wall — validate the trust problem specifically, add the insight that this is a data credibility issue not a tool issue
posts.draft_comment: The Excel thing isn't stubbornness — it's actually rational. People quote numbers in board meetings with their reputation on the line, and they'll only use a source they've personally stress-tested a hundred times. Power BI didn't fail, the trust-building process just never happened alongside the build. Did anyone on the finance team get involved before the dashboards went live, or was it more of a 'here's the thing we made' handover?

posts.post_text: Unpopular opinion: most operational dashboards are vanity projects. We had 47 KPIs on our ops dashboard. Nobody looked at it. Cut it to 5 metrics that actually drive decisions. Usage went from 10% to 85%. The problem with BI isn't the tools — it's that we measure everything and understand nothing.
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Director of Operations at Summit Group) engaging with a post about dashboard bloat — validate the 47-to-5 insight, add the 'decision vs. reporting' distinction, never pitch
posts.draft_comment: The jump from 10% to 85% usage tells you everything — those 5 metrics were probably the ones someone was already pulling manually in a spreadsheet before the dashboard existed. The KPI sprawl problem is almost always a political one, not a technical one. Everyone adds their metric so they feel counted, and suddenly the thing that was supposed to help make decisions just becomes a way to cover your back. Curious how you got the buy-in to actually cut 42 of them — that's usually the harder fight than building the dashboard in the first place.

posts.post_text: Hot take: self-service BI is a myth. We gave everyone Power BI licenses and what happened? 200 reports, zero consistency, three different definitions of 'revenue'. The promise of democratising data is great until you realise nobody agrees on what the data means. Build vs buy isn't the question — it's 'who owns the truth?'
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Innovation Director at NorthStar Retail) engaging on self-service BI chaos — validate the 'who owns truth' framing, add the layer that the tool was never the problem
posts.draft_comment: The 200 reports thing is so real — and the three definitions of revenue is usually where it all falls apart in a meeting. The tool didn't cause that though. The underlying problem is that nobody decided who gets to call the final number before they handed out the licenses. Who in your org actually has that authority right now?

posts.post_text: AI hallucinations in analytics are a security issue, not just an accuracy issue. If your AI tool generates a financial report with hallucinated numbers and someone makes a decision based on it, that's not a bug — it's a material risk. We need to start treating AI outputs with the same scrutiny as we treat user inputs.
posts.angle: CISO framing AI hallucinations as a security risk, with a CEO prospect engaging — validate the reframe, add the trust-chain insight that most analytics vendors are ignoring
posts.draft_comment: The security framing here is exactly right and most analytics vendors aren't ready for that conversation. The assumption has always been 'wrong number = fix the model' — but wrong number that reaches a CFO's deck unchallenged is a completely different category of problem. It's not just about the AI being wrong, it's about how many checkpoints between the model and the decision had any idea it could be wrong.

posts.post_text: Had a fascinating conversation with a client yesterday. They spent £200k on a BI platform and the only person who can use it is the one who built it. Self-service my arse. The gap between what vendors promise and what actually happens in a 50-person company is enormous. When will the industry admit that most BI tools are built for data teams, not business teams?
posts.angle: ICP prospect (COO at Sterling Consulting) engaging with a post about BI tools failing non-technical users — validate the core dysfunction with a specific observation, add a reframe about who BI is actually designed for
posts.draft_comment: The £200k number stings but honestly the real cost is the 49 people who quietly stopped asking questions because the tool made them feel stupid. Most BI platforms are built to impress buyers in a demo, not to answer a Tuesday afternoon question from someone in ops who just needs a straight answer. The 'self-service' label is doing a lot of heavy lifting for what's basically a sophisticated dashboard only a data analyst can touch. Wonder how many renewals actually get driven by the one person who built it rather than the team who was supposed to benefit.

posts.post_text: Just had our quarterly review and the CFO asked why the numbers in our BI dashboard don't match the numbers in the ERP. Turns out three different teams were applying different filters to the same dataset. AI won't fix this. Culture will. But nobody wants to hear that.
posts.angle: Commercial Director at a likely mid-market manufacturer has surfaced a classic data trust breakdown — validate the real diagnosis (governance, not culture) and add a sharper frame without pitching
posts.draft_comment: The CFO not trusting the dashboard is usually the symptom everyone sees. The cause is almost always that nobody agreed on the definitions before the data went in — what counts as revenue, which date field matters, does 'active customer' mean last 30 days or last 90. Culture gets blamed but it's really just that the unglamorous setup work got skipped. Does your team even have a shared glossary written down anywhere?

posts.post_text: Rolled out Copilot to 500 users last quarter. Usage after 90 days? 12%. The problem isn't the tool — it's that nobody knows what to ask it. We're essentially paying for a very expensive autocomplete. Shadow AI is the real story here — people are using ChatGPT on their phones because Copilot is too locked down.
posts.angle: IT Director surfacing real enterprise AI adoption failure — validate the 'nobody knows what to ask' root cause with a sharper reframe, no pitch needed
posts.draft_comment: The 12% number is brutal but honestly pretty standard. The dirty secret is that most people don't have a clear enough question in their head before they open the tool — and if the tool can't help them figure out what to even ask, they just go back to whatever felt easier. Shadow AI filling that gap makes total sense. The question isn't really 'how do we get people to use Copilot more' — it's why do your analysts know what questions to bring to it and nobody else does?
